content: Acute viral nasopharyngitis, commonly referred to as the common cold, is a highly contagious viral infection of the upper respiratory tract. It is most frequently caused by rhinoviruses, though other viruses such as coronaviruses and picornaviruses can also be responsible. The typical symptoms include a sore throat, runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, and coughing. These may sometimes be accompanied by systemic symptoms such as muscle aches, fatigue, malaise, headache, muscle weakness, or loss of appetite. Fever and severe exhaustion are more characteristic of influenza rather than the common cold. Symptoms of the common cold generally resolve within one week but can persist for up to 14 days. Infants and young children may experience more severe symptoms. Although the disease is usually mild and self-limiting, it often prompts patients to seek medical attention, use over-the-counter medications, and miss work or school. The economic burden of the common cold in the United States is substantial, amounting to billions of dollars annually. There are currently no vaccines available to prevent the common cold. The primary preventive measure is regular handwashing to reduce person-to-person transmission. No antiviral drugs have been approved for the treatment or cure of the common cold, and most available medications are palliative, addressing symptoms rather than the underlying infection. High doses of vitamin C, echinacea preparations, and zinc gluconate have been studied as potential treatments, but none have been approved by regulatory agencies such as the FDA or the European Medicines Agency. Historically, the common cold was first recognized as a distinct diagnosis by Benjamin Franklin in the 18th century. There is no established classification system for acute viral nasopharyngitis. Rhinoviruses, the most common cause of the common cold, are typically transmitted via aerosols generated by coughing or sneezing. The virus usually enters the body through the nasal passages but can also gain entry via the lacrimal ducts. Once inside, the virus invades epithelial cells, triggering the release of inflammatory cytokines, which are responsible for the symptoms of the common cold. The immune system responds through both cellular and humoral mechanisms, with bacterial flora also playing a role in defense against the virus. The primary cause of acute viral nasopharyngitis is rhinovirus infection. Other common viral causes include coronaviruses, human parainfluenza viruses, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). It is important to differentiate acute viral nasopharyngitis from other conditions that present with similar symptoms, such as influenza, allergic rhinitis, and acute sinusitis. Acute viral nasopharyngitis is the most common human infection worldwide and accounts for approximately half of all visits to family physicians. Adults typically experience 2–3 episodes per year, while children may have 6–10 infections annually. Among every 1,000 family physician visits, 500 are due to acute viral nasopharyngitis. Males are more frequently affected than females, and Native Americans are more prone to complications. Risk factors for acute viral nasopharyngitis include close contact with infected individuals, attendance at daycare centers, allergic rhinitis, and immunocompromised states. While the common cold tends to follow a seasonal pattern, there is no proven link between cold exposure or chilling and the occurrence of colds. If left untreated, the common cold resolves completely within 7–10 days. Common complications include sinusitis, otitis media, and exacerbation of reactive airway disease. The prognosis is excellent, with 50% of patients recovering within 7 days and 90% recovering within 15 days. The clinical presentation of acute viral nasopharyngitis includes symptoms such as a runny nose, cough, and sore throat. On physical examination, patients often appear unwell, with findings such as a runny nose, hyperemic nasal mucosa, and mild cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory findings consistent with acute viral nasopharyngitis include positive viral cultures, positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests, and leukocytosis on complete blood count (CBC). Imaging studies, such as X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, or ultrasounds, do not typically reveal findings associated with this condition. The primary treatment for acute viral nasopharyngitis is symptomatic management using palliative measures such as adequate fluid intake, rest, and throat sprays. Analgesics, nasal decongestants, and cough suppressants may be used to alleviate symptoms. Antibiotics are not effective, as the condition is viral in origin, and no antiviral drugs have been approved for its treatment. Despite popular belief, high doses of vitamin C, zinc, and steam inhalation have not been proven to be beneficial in treating the common cold. Surgical intervention is not recommended for the management of acute viral nasopharyngitis. Preventive measures include avoiding close contact with infected individuals and practicing regular handwashing to reduce the risk of transmission.
